result:
The proposed answer is incorrect because it counts every spine level as a cut time, when only a fraction 1−λ of them are.

**Where the solution goes wrong.** The solution claims that a cut time occurs for essentially every spine level, so that M(N) ≈ n(N) − O(1). That is false.

A cut time at k requires X_k to be a vertex not visited before, and the future never to return to any past vertex. The cut times are therefore the times of first arrival at a spine vertex (i+1,0), from (i,0), such that the walk never returns to (i,0) afterwards. (A cut time cannot lie inside a finite branch, since the walk must come back through the spine.)

**Probability of a cut at each level.** The spine-projected walk has right-step probability p = 1/(1+λ) and left-step probability q = λ/(1+λ). Excursions into branches always return to the same spine vertex, so they do not change this. The probability of ever returning from i+1 to i is q/p = λ. So level i yields a cut time with probability 1−λ, not 1. By ergodicity (the cut levels form a stationary, renewal-like pattern), the density of cut levels along the spine is 1−λ. Hence M(N) ≈ (1−λ)·n(N), where n(N) is the maximal spine level reached by time N.

**Growth of n(N).** The solution's estimate here is correct. The time to climb out of a branch of depth i against its drift is of order λ^{-i}. The time to reach level n is therefore of order λ^{-n}, up to subexponential fluctuations. This gives n(N) ~ log N / log(1/λ).

**Correct limit.** Combining the two factors gives

lim M(N)/log N = (1−λ)/(−log λ) = (1−λ)/log(1/λ),

which differs from the proposed answer 1/(−log λ) by the factor (1−λ).

VERDICT: REJECT
